title: An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning

Title:An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning
View PDF
            Abstract:Most systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning are in the same class as multi-layer perceptrons: while they may be universal function approximators, they struggle to learn associative tasks which are easy for transformers. Equilibrium propagation relies on a bidirectional flow of information through the physical system between input and output. The reverse flow is broken by more complex nonlinear systems, such as those performing multiplication which is needed to express dot-product attention. Here we explicitly restore this bidirectional flow by introducing extra circuit elements for this purpose into a double or dyadic circuit. We then use these ideas to construct an attention mechanism exploiting the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. We show that in simulations this circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task, despite using realistic reverse components which transmit only an approximate gradient. For this training to succeed we need cross-entropy loss (not mean squared error). We generate nudges appropriate for this loss using a novel floating circuit element, based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. We train the resistors in this circuit using the Lion optimiser, which can be implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates.

report.summary: A simulated all-transistor physical-learning transformer uses MOSFET-based attention and restored bidirectional gradients to learn a simple in-context task.
report.background: Physical learning aims to train circuits through local electrical dynamics rather than global backpropagation, promising low-power, adaptive hardware. Equilibrium propagation and coupled learning have trained energy-based physical systems, but mostly as multilayer perceptrons. They struggle with associative tasks that transformers handle easily because attention requires multiplication and dot products, which break the reverse information flow needed for gradient estimates. This paper addresses that bottleneck by adding circuit elements to a double or dyadic circuit to restore bidirectional flow. It exploits the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFETs to build attention and softmax, then trains resistors in simulation on a simple in-context learning task. The work sits at the intersection of neuromorphic computing, analog circuit design, and transformer algorithms.
key_points: The authors build an all-transistor attention mechanism using the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. This lets the circuit approximate softmax and dot-product-like operations directly in analog hardware, rather than emulating them digitally. The design is trained via physical-learning nudges, not standard backpropagation, and is evaluated in simulation.

A key obstacle is reverse gradient flow: nonlinear operations such as multiplication break equilibrium propagation's bidirectional information path. The paper restores this flow by introducing extra elements into a double or dyadic circuit. Even though the reverse components transmit only an approximate gradient, the authors show training can still succeed on their task.

Training requires cross-entropy loss rather than mean squared error. To generate appropriate nudges, the authors create a novel floating circuit element based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. This links the loss function, attention nonlinearity, and physical device physics in one co-design.

The circuit's resistors are trained with the Lion optimizer, implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates. This keeps optimization on or near the hardware, avoiding a separate digital optimizer. It suggests a path toward fully local, low-power training in analog transformer-like circuits.

In simulations, the circuit learns a simple in-context learning task despite approximate gradients and realistic reverse components. The result is a proof of concept, not a fabricated large-scale chip. Scaling to many layers, tokens, and parameters, and comparing against digital transformers, remains future work.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this points toward analog or neuromorphic transformers that could train and adapt on-chip with far less energy than GPU-based backpropagation. It also strengthens the case for co-designing algorithms with device physics, since choices like cross-entropy and Lion were necessary for physical training to work. Developers may eventually build models using local learning rules, capacitor-based optimizer state, and MOSFET attention primitives, but today they would treat this as a research direction rather than a drop-in framework. Regular users could see long-term benefits in private, low-power personal AI and adaptive edge devices, though near-term products are unlikely because results are simulation-only and limited to a simple task.
report.tools: Follow equilibrium propagation and coupled learning repositories on GitHub, plus PyTorch or JAX for prototyping physical-learning rules. For circuit-level simulation, explore ngspice, Xyce, or LTspice for MOSFET sub-threshold behavior. IBM's Analog Hardware Acceleration Kit (AIHWKit), MemTorch, and NeuroSim help model analog in-memory and neuromorphic training. Also watch the Lion optimizer implementation in PyTorch and open-source softmax/attention circuit demos.
